opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated strategic questions in the whole field, because it's fundamentally a portfolio problem and people tend to treat it as a binary.

The way I think about it is that your big scaled run is essentially a bet that your current recipe is good enough that the marginal compute is better spent realizing it than improving it. And for a lot of history that's been a pretty good bet: scaling laws are remarkably reliable, so if you have a recipe that works, putting more FLOPs into it gives you a predictable return. Research compute, by contrast, has a very fat-tailed return distribution. Most experiments tell you nothing, or tell you something you sort of already knew, and then occasionally one of them gives you a multiplier on effective compute that's worth more than an entire extra generation of hardware.

So the trap on one side is the team that's always scaling and never discovering. They ship on schedule, but they're compounding a recipe that's slowly falling behind, and eventually someone else finds a 2x or 3x algorithmic improvement and your giant run looks expensive for what it is. The trap on the other side is the team that's perpetually de-risking, always running one more ablation, and never actually commits. And there are things you only learn at scale. Some instabilities, some data effects, some capabilities just don't show up in small runs. So the big run is also a research experiment in its own right, which people forget.

What I'd advocate is a few things. First, a pretty meaningful chunk of compute, call it a substantial minority, should be protected for research, and protected in the sense that it doesn't get raided every time the main run wants more. Because the main run always wants more. Second, the research compute should be organized around a ladder of scales. You want ideas to be cheap to test at small scale, and then you need a disciplined process for promoting them up: does this hold at 10x, at 100x? Most of the craft is in knowing which small-scale results are going to transfer and which are artifacts. Teams that have a really good intuition for that, and really good infrastructure for running clean comparisons, effectively have way more compute than their raw FLOP count suggests.

And third, I think the iteration speed of researchers matters enormously. If a good researcher has to wait days to get signal, you've basically cut their productivity by an order of magnitude. So sometimes the right allocation isn't more total research compute, it's making sure the people with the best taste get fast turnaround on their experiments.

The honest answer is the ratio isn't fixed. Early in a paradigm, when there's tons of low-hanging fruit, you should skew heavily toward research. When a recipe is mature and you've wrung out most of the obvious gains, you skew toward scaling. The hard part is noticing which regime you're in, because it changes, and new paradigms like RL on top of pre-trained models reset that clock.

r001.rationale: It says some instabilities, data effects, and capabilities appear only at scale, and that these may not show up in small runs.

r002.rationale: It warns that small-scale results can be artifacts and may not transfer, but does not state that improving compute efficiency in research can steer development toward approaches that fail to scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions a lab has to answer, and most people underrate how hard it is. The naive framing is that you've got a fixed pool of compute and you split it, some fraction goes to the big run and some fraction goes to the research cluster. But in practice the two are much more entangled than that.

The way I think about it is that the big run is where you cash out everything you've learned, and the research compute is where you buy the options on the next run. If you put everything into scaling the thing you already know works, you get a very predictable improvement, basically whatever the scaling laws tell you. But you've learned nothing about the next step, and you're just hoping the curve continues. If you put too much into research, you've got a lot of interesting small-scale results and nothing that's actually frontier, and a lot of those results won't transfer anyway.

The thing that makes this genuinely difficult is that the value of research compute is incredibly uneven. Most experiments don't pan out. But the ones that do, the right data mix, the right architectural tweak, a better optimizer, those can be worth more than a whole generation of scaling. So you're trading a certain return against a very heavy-tailed one. And the heavy tail is where all the real progress has come from historically. Nobody got to where we are just by making the same thing bigger.

So practically I'd say a few things. One, you want your research to be done at a scale where results actually transfer. A lot of compute gets wasted on experiments at a size where the conclusions just don't hold at the frontier. It's often better to run fewer experiments at a more meaningful scale than hundreds of tiny ones. Two, you want very tight feedback loops between the research teams and the people running the big job, so what gets learned actually makes it in. And three, the fraction should probably be larger than feels comfortable. I think the instinct is always to pull compute towards the flagship because that's what's visible and that's what ships, but the labs that have done best over the last few years are the ones that protected the research budget even when it was painful.

The other thing I'd add is that the "best existing approach" is a bit of a moving target. By the time the big run finishes, you've usually figured out three things you wish you'd done differently. So in some sense every big run is itself an experiment, just an extremely expensive one. And you want to design it so you're learning as much as possible, not just producing a model.

r001.rationale: The response says experiments at a size where conclusions do not hold at the frontier can waste compute, and recommends research at a scale where results transfer. This communicates that small-scale experiments can miss behavior relevant to large runs.

r002.rationale: The response warns that small-scale results may not transfer to the frontier, but does not state that improving compute efficiency within a research regime can steer development toward approaches that fail to scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much runway you have for research to change the next big run. If you’re about to launch it, you should mostly be scaling something you understand. If you have six months, spending all your compute on the current best recipe seems like a mistake, because a modest improvement in efficiency could pay for the entire research budget.

The tricky part is that you need experiments at a scale where the results are informative. You can do an enormous number of tiny experiments and become very confident about what works on tiny models. That doesn’t necessarily tell you what to do on your biggest model. So I’d want a lot of cheap exploration, then a fairly ruthless process for taking promising ideas up in scale and checking whether the gains survive.

I wouldn’t pick a fixed percentage in the abstract. I’d ask: what are the unresolved decisions for the next run, which experiments could change those decisions, and what would that change be worth? You also need some room for research that doesn’t have an obvious immediate payoff. Otherwise, you end up optimizing the recipe you already have forever.

r001.rationale: It says tiny-model results may not inform decisions for the biggest model and recommends scaling promising ideas to check whether their gains persist.

r002.rationale: It does not say that improving compute efficiency in research can steer development toward approaches that fail to scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to frame it is: how much compute would you spend to find an improvement that makes the rest of your compute more valuable? If you can get a 20% efficiency improvement, that’s a huge return when you apply it to a much larger training run. So even experiments that look expensive in isolation can be very cheap relative to their potential payoff.

The difficulty is that you don’t know which results will transfer. You can have something that works beautifully at a small scale and disappears when you scale it up. So you need a ladder of experiments where you’re testing ideas cheaply, then spending progressively more to establish that the promising ones actually work at the scale you care about.

I’d be suspicious of a fixed allocation like, ‘We always spend 10% on research.’ It depends on how much uncertainty there is in your recipe and how good your next research opportunities are. If you’ve got a queue of compelling experiments, you should probably spend more. If you’re mostly turning knobs and getting nothing, you should probably scale what works.

There’s also a timing issue. An improvement discovered after you’ve started the big run might not help that run at all. So the question isn’t just how much compute you allocate to research. It’s whether you can get the evidence in time to change the decision.

r001.rationale: It says an approach can work at small scale and disappear when scaled up, and recommends testing promising ideas at the scale of interest.

r002.rationale: It notes that small-scale results may not transfer, but does not say that improving compute efficiency in research can steer development toward approaches that fail to scale.
